parsed.explanation: The combined regime pairs a protective division with a hostile federal layer the division cannot displace. Entry is the sharpest exposure: federal screening instructs officers to refuse cases where documents cast doubt on sex and to consider fraud-based lifetime ineligibility — a universal, traveler-facing measure with no documented remedy. Federal orders bar trans people from government-funded single-sex facilities and reshape national custody toward conversion-style practice; neither is offset by the division's statutes. The division itself documents real operative protections: public-accommodation and housing anti-discrimination, constitutional equality amendment, hate-crime penalties with a hotline, surgery-free marker changes including X markers, mandated care coverage, and a low-risk band placement. No division-specific violence or facility-ban entry is documented — an open question, not safety. For a minor, federal youth-care hostility and document rules compound the parent's exposure while state care mandates pull partly the other way.

entry_documents.exposure: Federal February 2025 cable instructs refusal where documents cast reasonable doubt on sex and referral for fraud-based lifetime ineligibility; X markers barred for new issues; trans travelers report passports blocked or confiscated. Universal entry-stage exposure.
entry_documents.protection: Challenges pending in national courts; existing mismatched-marker passports valid until expiry; legal-aid FAQ on document rules. Division offers X markers on its own IDs, but entry is federal.
entry_documents.interaction: A trans visitor's foreign documents meet federal adjudication regardless of division protections; a document discrepancy can escalate to refusal or a fraud finding the division cannot review.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: Federal corrections bureau adopted conversion-style policies from 2026 (hair cutting, hormone removal, substituted psychiatric drugs); immigration custody reports forced labour, beatings, solitary, sexual abuse of trans detainees; prisoner counts no longer reported.
investigation_detention_custody.protection: Division has a 2023 law explicitly protecting trans and intersex people in state/province correctional facilities.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: State custody protection does not reach federal immigration or national custody; the July 2026 assessment still rates the division short on incarcerated-trans protection, so even state practice is weaker than its text.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: Federal executive order bars trans people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with identity. Nationally, 21 state/provinces ban identity-congruent facility use in government buildings; 4 criminalise it in some circumstances; one documented arrest under such a law (March 2025, trespass, held in men's ward).
federal_state_facilities.protection: Division has public-accommodations protections (2011/2017) and a constitutional equality amendment (2022) covering gender identity/expression.
federal_state_facilities.interaction: Division accommodation law plausibly shelters private venues but cannot override the federal facility order in federal buildings; whether the division itself appears on the facilities map is not reproduced — status uncertain, not evidence of a ban or of safety.

care_services.exposure: Federal orders and proposed rules target gender-affirming care, youth care declared constitutional to ban by a June 2025 ruling, subpoenas of under-19 patient records, and LGBTQ youth lifeline shutdown.
care_services.protection: Division mandates insurer and public-programme coverage of medically necessary gender-affirming treatment (effective January 2024); conversion therapy on minors banned; care access is a documented state protection for visitors needing care.
care_services.interaction: A visiting minor's care sits at the clash point: state mandates coverage while federal policy hostility and record subpoenas create chilling exposure the division cannot shield.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: Federal counterterrorism strategy targets groups 'radically pro-transgender'; DOJ reward memo frames 'radical gender ideology' among violent-extremist animating views; officials describe care as mutilation; 66% public support for birth-sex document rules.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: Division's hate-crime statute covers gender identity/expression (2013) with a reporting hotline (January 2025); 2025 assessment places division in low-risk band; state officials protective.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: Federal framing raises outing probability and discourages reporting, while division institutions counter locally; the division's tone does not alter federal adjudication or custody.

minors_guardians.exposure: Federal order directs criminal investigation of schools facilitating social transition and funding revocation; youth-care bans upheld federally; birth-sex eligibility rules for school sports adopted by the division's activities association (April 2025).
minors_guardians.protection: Division school anti-bullying law lists gender identity (2015); 2026 sports ballot initiative failed; care-coverage mandate in force.
minors_guardians.interaction: A travelling family's minor faces federal document and framing exposure plus division-level school/sport rules that are resident-facing; parent's own passport discrepancy at entry is the shared entry risk.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: National hate-crime statistics show persistent bias incidents; the division's inventory contains no dated, dated-outcome incident of anti-trans violence — absence in a well-documented record is weakly positive, not proof of safety.
street_violence_police_response.protection: Division hate-crime penalties, hotline, robust non-discrimination policies, national hate-crime statute covering gender identity; July 2026 assessment credits fairly robust protections.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: State recourse is real but partial: 23 of the units cover gender identity in bias statutes, and the division is one of them, improving response relative to most units.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: Federal passport and order challenges remain unresolved; exposure varies by moment of travel; federal facility rule and custody policies operate without documented relief.
remedies_unknowns.protection: Division documents functioning protections: constitutional amendment, enforcement-capable anti-discrimination law, low-risk band; several federal orders enjoined.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: Remedies work at the division level but the operative federal layer supplies no effective counterweight; the division's protections raise the floor without curing the entry and federal-custody exposures.

anchor_checks.comparison: Like 0.45-A, a federal birth-sex facility rule reaches publicly funded buildings with no documented exemption for visitors, while the wider society is polite and some levels are protective. This case adds federal entry-refusal and custody exposures, but also stronger division-level service and care protections than Denvara shows — so it sits near, not below, this anchor.

Teravi's hostilities are local operator refusals with partial mediation and a thin custody record. Here documented harms are federal and institutional (entry fraud referrals, custody conversion practice, facility bans), which outrank scattered operator hostility; division protections roughly match Teravi's provincial mediators. Net: slightly below 0.55-B.

Ilvora pairs acceptance, accepted documents and working compensation with only an open custody question. This dossier has documented universal federal entry and facility exposures with no working remedy — a tier-1 feature absent in 0.75-C. Materially lower despite excellent division statutes.

parsed.synthesis: The traveller meets two systems at once. The federal layer supplies universal, unremedied exposures: document scrutiny with refusal and fraud-referral instructions at entry, a birth-sex facility rule for government-funded spaces, conversion-style national custody practice, and hostile official framing — none of which the division can displace. The division supplies genuine operative protections a visitor can actually use: public-accommodation and housing guarantees, constitutional equality, hate-crime penalties with a hotline, surgery-free marker changes, mandated care coverage, and a low-risk assessment band. Those protections meaningfully cushion hotels, restaurants, shops, state services and emergencies, and the absence of documented division violence in a well-documented record is mildly positive. But they do not reach the border desk, federal buildings' single-sex facilities, or federal custody, and the division's own facilities-map entry is missing — an open question. For an unaccompanied adult the score sits in elevated risk; for a traveller with a minor, federal youth-care and document hostility adds weight. The combined picture is protected on the street, exposed at the border and in federal institutions: above the 0.45 anchors only because the division's protections demonstrably operate, below 0.55 because the federal universal exposures carry no documented remedy.
